messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: massive doc reargue?
parts:
I'm concerned about duplicated effort if we start focusing
on a best practices Wiki.

The manual now has roughly 5 components

I. Programming Guide
Chapters 1 - 21, Appendices B, C
225 pages

II. Language Specification
Chapters 22 - 28, parts of 54, 55, Appendix D
100 pages

III. Built-in Function Guide
Chapters 29 - 35
125 pages

III. Bayes, MLE, and MCMC
Chapters 52 - 54
25 pages

IV. Algorithms
Chapters 56, 57, 58
15 pages

V. Software Process
Chapter 59
10 pages

There's also an appendix on licensing and a bibliography.

* Michael wants to rewrite Algorithms

* Andrew wants to restart the programming guide as a Wiki

* We can break out the process as a separate doc a la R

* The manual can then be reduced to just the language spec
and functions

* We can just scrap the intro to Bayes and MLE (though it'd
be nice to have something free to distribute as an alternative
to always telling people to buy BDA)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] massive doc reargue?
parts:
> On Apr 8, 2015, at 4:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> III [Bayes, MCMC, MLE] also needs a rewrite, in particular one that introduces some

> subtle concepts like density vs measure and the typical set
> in order to prepare readers for trickier theoretical concepts like
> ergodicty and ergodicity-related pathologies.

That's where you come in!

The question is whether we put this in a book, standalone doc,
on a Wiki, or what. I guess writing it first is a good start, but
I think where we target might inform that.

> It might be
> worth having an expository doc with
>
> Intro to Bayes and MCMC
> Algorithms (expository)
> Intro to Language
> Programming Guide
> Recommended Style and Software Process
>
> and then a reference guide with
>
> Algorithms (detailed)
> Complete Language Spec
> Function Guide

That makes sense to me. It would also make sense to break out
by topic with each part having an introduction and then advanced
part.

What I'm really thinking is that we need to write the ultimate
series on Probability, Statistics, and Computation, with each having
an introductory and advanced book targeting a semester-long course,
and then a single overview. That's seven books in total:

Getting Started with Probability, Statistics, and Computation

Intro to Prob Theory
Intro to Applied Stats
Intro to Stat Computation

Prob theory
Applied Stats
Stat Computation


Then, on top of that, the Stan language reference.

Now all we need is half a dozen years of funding to carry it out
without distractions.

- Bob
